specStatements.text: The nucleus of a cell contains chromosomes made of DNA molecules. Each chromosome carries a large number of genes.
In body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs.
Cells divide in a series of stages called the cell cycle. Students should be able to describe the stages of the cell cycle, including mitosis.
During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.
Before a cell can divide it needs to grow and increase the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. The DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
In mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
Finally the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.
Students need to understand the three overall stages of the cell cycle but do not need to know the different phases of the mitosis stage.
Cell division by mitosis is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms.
Students should be able to recognise and describe situations in given contexts where mitosis is occurring.
A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.
Students should be able to describe the function of stem cells in embryos, in adult animals and in the meristems in plants.
Stem cells from human embryos can be cloned and made to differentiate into most different types of human cells.
Stem cells from adult bone marrow can form many types of cells including blood cells.
Meristem tissue in plants can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the life of the plant.
Knowledge and understanding of stem cell techniques are not required.
Treatment with stem cells may be able to help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis.
In therapeutic cloning an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient. Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body so they may be used for medical treatment.
The use of stem cells has potential risks such as transfer of viral infection, and some people have ethical or religious objections.

Stem cells from meristems in plants can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically. Rare species can be cloned to protect from extinction.; Crop plants with special features such as disease resistance can be cloned to produce large numbers of identical plants for farmers.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Everything here is written around the three overall stages of the cell cycle only: (1) the cell grows and increases its sub-cellular structures while the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome, (2) mitosis, in which one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides, and (3) division of the cytoplasm and cell membranes to form two identical cells. No named sub-phases of the mitosis stage are introduced, defined or tested anywhere in the concepts, misconceptions or questions.

Stem cell items are limited to what a stem cell is, where stem cells are found (embryos, adult bone marrow, plant meristems), what they can differentiate into, their uses in treatment and in cloning plants, and the risks and objections. No stem cell techniques are described or tested: nothing covers how stem cells are extracted, cultured, cloned in the laboratory or transplanted.

concepts.definition: A structure found in the nucleus of a cell, made of a DNA molecule. Each chromosome carries a large number of genes.
A section of a DNA molecule carried on a chromosome. A single chromosome carries a large number of genes, so genes are much smaller structures than chromosomes.

concepts.term: Pairs of chromosomes in body cells
concepts.definition: In body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs, so each type of chromosome is present twice in the nucleus.

The series of stages in which cells divide. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells. The three overall stages are growth with DNA replication, mitosis, and division of the cytoplasm and cell membranes.

concepts.term: Growth stage of the cell cycle
concepts.definition: Before a cell can divide it needs to grow and increase the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. In this stage the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
The stage of the cell cycle in which one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.

concepts.term: Division of the cytoplasm and cell membranes
concepts.definition: The final stage of the cell cycle, in which the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.
Cell division by mitosis is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms, because it produces new cells that are identical to the parent cell.
An undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.
Stem cells from human embryos, which can be cloned and made to differentiate into most different types of human cells.

concepts.term: Adult stem cells in bone marrow
concepts.definition: Stem cells from adult bone marrow, which can form many types of cells including blood cells.
Tissue in plants that can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the life of the plant.
A process in which an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient. Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body so they may be used for medical treatment.

Stem cells from meristems in plants can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically. Rare species can be cloned to protect them from extinction, and crop plants with special features such as disease resistance can be cloned to produce large numbers of identical plants for farmers.

misconceptions.question: How many genes does one chromosome carry?
misconceptions.misconception: Each chromosome carries just one gene, so a gene and a chromosome are really the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook diagrams often label a single chromosome with one gene to keep the picture simple, and the two words are used in the same sentence so often that students treat them as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus of a cell contains chromosomes made of DNA molecules, and each chromosome carries a large number of genes.

misconceptions.question: Which is the larger structure, a gene or a chromosome?
misconceptions.correct: A chromosome, because one chromosome carries a large number of genes.
misconceptions.misconception: A gene is the larger structure and contains many chromosomes inside it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet the word gene first and in everyday language, so it feels like the 'big' idea, and the hierarchy of nucleus, chromosome, gene is easily reversed.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus of a cell contains chromosomes made of DNA molecules, and each chromosome carries a large number of genes, so the chromosome is the larger structure.

misconceptions.question: How are the chromosomes arranged in a body cell?
misconceptions.correct: They are normally found in pairs.
misconceptions.misconception: Chromosomes in body cells are single and unpaired, so a human body cell holds 46 unrelated chromosomes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams of the cell cycle usually draw chromosomes singly and scattered, and students count the total number without noticing that they match up as pairs.
misconceptions.correction: In body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs.

misconceptions.question: When does a cell copy its DNA?
misconceptions.correct: Before mitosis, during the growth stage of the cell cycle.
misconceptions.misconception: The cell cycle is just mitosis, so a cell divides straight away without first growing and replicating its DNA.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mitosis is the stage that is drawn, animated and named most often, so the growth stage before it is treated as a gap rather than as a stage of the cell cycle.
misconceptions.correction: Before a cell can divide it needs to grow and increase the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. The DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.

misconceptions.question: How many chromosomes does each new cell have after mitosis?
misconceptions.correct: The same number as the parent cell.
misconceptions.misconception: Mitosis halves the number of chromosomes, so each new cell ends up with half of the parent cell's chromosomes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One cell becomes two, so students assume everything inside is shared out and halved, forgetting that the genetic material was doubled first.
misconceptions.correction: During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells, and in mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.

misconceptions.question: How do the two cells produced by mitosis compare?
misconceptions.correct: They are identical to each other and to the parent cell.
misconceptions.misconception: The two cells produced by mitosis are genetically different from each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link cell division with the production of offspring, which they know vary, so they expect variation whenever cells divide.
misconceptions.correction: During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.

misconceptions.question: Is cell division finished once the nucleus has divided?
misconceptions.correct: No, the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide afterwards.
misconceptions.misconception: Cell division is complete as soon as the nucleus has divided, so the cytoplasm and cell membranes do not need to divide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mitosis is presented as the dramatic, well illustrated part of the cell cycle, so the final stage is easily left off the end of a description.
misconceptions.correction: Finally the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.

misconceptions.question: Does mitosis still happen in a fully grown adult?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, new identical cells are still produced by mitosis.
misconceptions.misconception: Mitosis stops once an organism has finished growing, so it happens in embryos and children but not in adults.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mitosis is introduced as the process behind growth, so students tie it to a period of getting bigger rather than to the production of new identical cells.
misconceptions.correction: Cell division by mitosis is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms and it continues in adults: for example, stem cells from adult bone marrow form many types of cells including blood cells.

misconceptions.question: What kind of cell is a stem cell?
misconceptions.misconception: A stem cell is a specialised cell with its own particular job, like a nerve cell or a muscle cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Stem cells are taught alongside lists of specialised cells, so students file them as one more cell type with a function rather than as cells that have not yet differentiated.
misconceptions.correction: A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.

misconceptions.question: What can stem cells from adult bone marrow form?
misconceptions.correct: Many types of cells, including blood cells.
misconceptions.misconception: Stem cells from adult bone marrow can differentiate into any type of cell, in exactly the same way as stem cells from embryos.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both sources are called stem cells, so students assume the two must be able to do the same job and ignore the difference in wording between the two statements.
misconceptions.correction: Stem cells from human embryos can be cloned and made to differentiate into most different types of human cells, while stem cells from adult bone marrow can form many types of cells including blood cells.

misconceptions.question: When can meristem tissue produce new plant cells?
misconceptions.correct: Throughout the life of the plant.
misconceptions.misconception: Meristem tissue can produce new cells while a plant is young, and stops working once the plant is mature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer what they know about animals, which reach a final adult size, onto plants, and assume plant growth must also stop.
misconceptions.correction: Meristem tissue in plants can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the life of the plant.

misconceptions.question: Are stem cells from therapeutic cloning rejected by the patient?
misconceptions.correct: No, because the embryo has the same genes as the patient.
misconceptions.misconception: Stem cells produced by therapeutic cloning are rejected by the patient's body, just like a transplanted organ.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that transplants are often rejected, and apply that rule to every cell or tissue that is put into a patient without checking whose genes the cells carry.
misconceptions.correction: In therapeutic cloning an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient. Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body so they may be used for medical treatment.

misconceptions.question: What are the drawbacks of using stem cells?
misconceptions.correct: There are potential risks such as transfer of viral infection, as well as ethical or religious objections.
misconceptions.misconception: The drawbacks of using stem cells are ethical or religious ones, and there is no medical risk to the patient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Classroom discussion of stem cells concentrates on the debate about embryos, so the medical risk named in the specification is crowded out.
misconceptions.correction: The use of stem cells has potential risks such as transfer of viral infection, and some people have ethical or religious objections.

misconceptions.question: What can treatment with stem cells do for conditions such as diabetes and paralysis?
misconceptions.correct: It may be able to help these conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: Stem cell treatment is a guaranteed cure for conditions such as diabetes and paralysis.
misconceptions.whyItArises: News reports describe promising individual cases as breakthroughs, and the specification's careful wording 'may be able to help' is easily overstated in an answer.
misconceptions.correction: Treatment with stem cells may be able to help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis.

misconceptions.question: How quickly and cheaply can plants be cloned from meristems?
misconceptions.misconception: Cloning plants from meristem stem cells is a slow and expensive process.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate the word cloning with complicated animal cloning in laboratories, and do not connect it with the routine, cheap propagation of plants.
misconceptions.correction: Stem cells from meristems in plants can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically, so rare species can be cloned to protect them from extinction and crop plants with special features such as disease resistance can be cloned in large numbers for farmers.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about chromosomes and genes in a body cell is correct?

options.text: A gene is made up of a large number of chromosomes.
options.rationale: A student who has reversed the hierarchy thinks the gene is the larger structure and holds chromosomes inside it. It is wrong because the chromosome is the DNA molecule and each chromosome carries a large number of genes.

options.text: Each chromosome carries one gene made of DNA.
options.rationale: A student who treats gene and chromosome as the same thing expects a one to one match. It is wrong because each chromosome carries a large number of genes, not one.

options.text: Each chromosome in the nucleus is found singly.
options.rationale: A student who pictures chromosomes as scattered single structures picks this. It is wrong because in body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs.

options.text: Each chromosome carries a large number of genes.
options.rationale: The nucleus of a cell contains chromosomes made of DNA molecules, and each chromosome carries a large number of genes.

mcqs.stem: How are the chromosomes normally arranged in a body cell?

options.text: Singly, inside the nucleus of the cell.
options.rationale: A student who believes chromosomes are single and unpaired picks this. It is wrong because in body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs.

options.text: In pairs, held inside the nucleus of the cell.
options.rationale: In body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs, and the chromosomes are contained in the nucleus of the cell.

options.text: In pairs, inside a large gene in the cell.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a gene contains chromosomes places the pair inside a gene. It is wrong because each chromosome carries a large number of genes, so genes are held on chromosomes.

options.text: In pairs, with a single gene per pair.
options.rationale: A student who believes one chromosome means one gene picks this. It is wrong because each chromosome carries a large number of genes.

mcqs.stem: Which description gives the three overall stages of the cell cycle in the correct order?

options.text: The cell grows and copies its DNA, the nucleus divides, then the cytoplasm divides.
options.rationale: Before a cell can divide it grows and the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome; in mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides; finally the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.

options.text: The nucleus divides first, then the cell grows and copies its DNA, then the cytoplasm divides.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the cell cycle is just mitosis puts the nucleus dividing first and treats growth as something that happens afterwards. It is wrong because before a cell can divide it needs to grow and the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.

options.text: The cell grows and halves its DNA, then the nucleus divides, then the cytoplasm divides.
options.rationale: A student who believes mitosis halves the chromosome number expects the DNA to be shared out rather than copied. It is wrong because the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.

options.text: The cell grows and copies its DNA, then the nucleus divides, and division is complete.
options.rationale: A student who stops at the nucleus dividing leaves out the last stage. It is wrong because finally the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.

mcqs.stem: A human body cell containing 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. What does each new cell contain?

options.text: 23 chromosomes, matching the parent cell
options.rationale: A student who believes mitosis halves the chromosome number shares the 46 chromosomes between the two cells. It is wrong because the genetic material is doubled first, so each new cell receives a full set of 46.

options.text: 46 chromosomes, not identical to the parent cell
options.rationale: A student who expects cell division to create variation keeps the number right but makes the cells differ. It is wrong because the genetic material is divided into two identical cells.

options.text: 46 chromosomes, identical to the parent cell
options.rationale: During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells, so each new cell has the parent cell's 46 chromosomes.

options.text: 23 chromosomes, different from the parent cell
options.rationale: A student who thinks the DNA is not replicated before division expects each cell to get part of the genetic material and so to differ. It is wrong because the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome before the cell divides.

mcqs.stem: Before a cell divides it grows and increases its number of ribosomes and mitochondria. What happens to the DNA at this stage?

options.text: The DNA is halved to leave one copy of each chromosome.
options.rationale: A student who believes mitosis halves the chromosome number expects the halving to happen to the DNA. It is wrong because the genetic material is doubled, not halved, before division.

options.text: The DNA replicates after the nucleus has divided in two.
options.rationale: A student who treats the cell cycle as just mitosis puts replication after the nucleus divides. It is wrong because the DNA replicates before the cell can divide, in the growth stage.

options.text: The DNA is altered so the two new cells are different.
options.rationale: A student who expects variation from cell division looks for a change in the DNA. It is wrong because the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.

options.text: The DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
options.rationale: Before a cell can divide the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome, which is how the genetic material is doubled.

mcqs.stem: What happens during mitosis and the stage that follows it?

options.text: One set of chromosomes goes to each end, then the cytoplasm divides.
options.rationale: In mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides; finally the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.

options.text: One set of chromosomes goes to each end, and the cell stays whole.
options.rationale: A student who thinks division is complete once the nucleus divides leaves the cell as one. It is wrong because finally the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.

options.text: Half of each chromosome goes to each end, then the cytoplasm divides.
options.rationale: A student who believes mitosis halves the genetic material splits the chromosomes themselves. It is wrong because one whole set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.

options.text: The chromosomes are shared unevenly, then the cytoplasm divides.
options.rationale: A student who expects the new cells to differ shares the chromosomes out unevenly. It is wrong because one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end, forming two identical cells.

mcqs.stem: A cut on the arm of a fully grown adult heals as new skin cells are produced. Which statement about the new cells is correct?

options.text: New cells with half the chromosomes are made.
options.rationale: A student who believes mitosis halves the chromosome number expects the new skin cells to have fewer chromosomes. It is wrong because the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.

options.text: The new identical cells are produced by mitosis.
options.rationale: Cell division by mitosis produces two identical cells and is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms, which includes producing new skin cells in this context.

options.text: New genetically different cells are made.
options.rationale: A student who links cell division with variation expects the replacement cells to differ. It is wrong because the genetic material is divided into two identical cells.

options.text: Mitosis has stopped because the adult is grown.
options.rationale: A student who ties mitosis to getting bigger rules it out in an adult. It is wrong because mitosis continues to produce new identical cells in adults, for example blood cells from stem cells in adult bone marrow.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a stem cell?

options.text: A specialised cell that carries out one particular function.
options.rationale: A student who has filed stem cells alongside nerve and muscle cells picks a specialised cell. It is wrong because a stem cell is an undifferentiated cell.

options.text: A bone marrow cell that forms most cell types in the body.
options.rationale: A student who thinks adult stem cells can do everything defines all stem cells this way. It is wrong because stem cells from adult bone marrow form many types of cells including blood cells, and stem cells are found in embryos and plant meristems too.

options.text: An undifferentiated cell that can give rise to other cells.
options.rationale: A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.

options.text: A meristem cell that makes new cells only while the plant is young.
options.rationale: A student who believes meristems only work while a plant is young builds that time limit into the definition. It is wrong because meristem tissue can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the life of the plant.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the function of stem cells is correct?

options.text: Meristem tissue can differentiate into any plant cell.
options.rationale: Meristem tissue in plants can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the life of the plant.

options.text: Bone marrow stem cells can differentiate into any type of cell.
options.rationale: A student who treats all stem cells as equivalent gives adult stem cells the full range. It is wrong because stem cells from adult bone marrow form many types of cells including blood cells, while embryonic stem cells can be made to differentiate into most different types of human cells.

options.text: Embryonic stem cells are specialised for one particular job.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a stem cell is a specialised cell applies that to the embryo. It is wrong because stem cells are undifferentiated, and those from human embryos can be made to differentiate into most different types of human cells.

options.text: Meristem tissue stops making new cells once the plant matures.
options.rationale: A student who transfers the idea of a final adult size from animals to plants picks this. It is wrong because meristem tissue can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the life of the plant.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about therapeutic cloning is correct?

options.text: The stem cells produced are rejected by the patient's body.
options.rationale: A student who applies the rule about transplant rejection to every treatment picks this. It is wrong because the embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient, so the stem cells are not rejected.

options.text: The stem cells are taken from the patient's bone marrow.
options.rationale: A student who thinks bone marrow stem cells can supply every treatment picks this. It is wrong because in therapeutic cloning the stem cells come from an embryo produced with the same genes as the patient.

options.text: An embryo with the same genes as the patient is produced.
options.rationale: In therapeutic cloning an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient, and stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body so they may be used for medical treatment.

options.text: The cells produced are specialised for one particular job.
options.rationale: A student who believes stem cells are already specialised picks this. It is wrong because the embryo provides undifferentiated stem cells from which other cells can arise by differentiation.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about treatment with stem cells is correct?

options.text: It is a guaranteed cure for conditions such as paralysis.
options.rationale: A student who has read about breakthroughs overstates what has been shown. It is wrong because treatment with stem cells may be able to help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis.

options.text: It uses bone marrow stem cells to replace nerve cells.
options.rationale: A student who thinks adult bone marrow stem cells can form any cell type picks this source. It is wrong because stem cells from adult bone marrow form many types of cells including blood cells.

options.text: It fails as the patient's body rejects the cells.
options.rationale: A student who assumes rejection is unavoidable rules the treatment out. It is wrong because stem cells from an embryo with the same genes as the patient are not rejected by the patient's body.

options.text: It may be able to help conditions such as paralysis.
options.rationale: Treatment with stem cells may be able to help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the risks of using stem cells is correct?

options.text: Viral infection could be transferred to the patient.
options.rationale: The use of stem cells has potential risks such as transfer of viral infection, and some people have ethical or religious objections.

options.text: The concerns are ethical rather than medical ones.
options.rationale: A student whose lessons focused on the debate about embryos overlooks the medical risk. It is wrong because the use of stem cells has potential risks such as transfer of viral infection as well as ethical or religious objections.

options.text: The cloned embryo's cells are rejected by the body.
options.rationale: A student who assumes all transplanted cells are rejected names that as the risk. It is wrong because an embryo produced with the same genes as the patient gives stem cells that are not rejected.

options.text: The cells cannot give rise to more cells of one type.
options.rationale: A student who thinks stem cells are already specialised doubts they can keep dividing. It is wrong because a stem cell is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type.

mcqs.stem: Why are stem cells from meristems used to clone rare plant species?

options.text: Different plants are produced quickly and economically.
options.rationale: A student who expects cell division to create variation thinks the new plants differ. It is wrong because clones produced from meristem stem cells are identical plants.

options.text: Identical plants are produced both quickly and economically.
options.rationale: Stem cells from meristems in plants can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically, so rare species can be cloned to protect them from extinction.

options.text: Identical plants are produced slowly and at high cost.
options.rationale: A student who links cloning with expensive laboratory work picks this. It is wrong because meristem stem cells produce clones of plants quickly and economically.

options.text: Identical plants are produced while the parent is young.
options.rationale: A student who thinks meristems work in young plants alone restricts when cloning is possible. It is wrong because meristem tissue can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the life of the plant.
